Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. New York is widely regarded as a cosmopolitan city, home to people from almost every nation on earth. — COSMOPOLITAN (adj) = đa văn hoá, sành điệu, cởi mở với nhiều nền văn hoá; collocation "a cosmopolitan city/outlook/mindset". Phân biệt với "multicultural" (nhấn mạnh sự cùng tồn tại của nhiều văn hoá, không nhất thiết mang sắc thái sành điệu).
2. Rising xenophobia in some countries is often driven by economic insecurity. — XENOPHOBIA (n) = tâm lý bài ngoại; chú ý phát âm chữ "x" đầu từ là /z/, không phải /ks/; trọng âm rơi vào "-PHO-".

3. Many critics warn against the creeping homogenisation of culture, where local traditions are replaced by standardised global norms. — HOMOGENISATION (n) = sự đồng nhất hoá văn hoá; collocation "cultural homogenisation", "drive homogenisation"; động từ là "homogenise".

4. The indigenous tribes who have lived in this region since ancient times still speak a language found nowhere else. — INDIGENOUS (adj) = bản địa, bản xứ; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai "-DIG-", âm "g" đọc mềm /dʒ/; collocation "indigenous communities/languages/traditions".

5. When immigrant families settle in a new country, their children often undergo a process of cultural assimilation. — ASSIMILATION (n) = sự đồng hoá văn hoá; phân biệt với "integration" (hoà nhập nhưng vẫn giữ bản sắc riêng); động từ "assimilate (into)".

6. Under the pressure of globalised consumer culture, local dialects and customs are suffering steady erosion. — EROSION (n) = sự mai một, xói mòn (giá trị/truyền thống); collocation "the erosion of traditional values", "cultural erosion"; động từ "erode".

7. Governments should protect not just physical artefacts but also intangible heritage such as folklore, dialects and rituals. — INTANGIBLE HERITAGE (n phrase) = di sản văn hoá phi vật thể; đối lập với "tangible heritage" (di tích, công trình vật thể); collocation "safeguard/preserve intangible heritage".

8. Exposure to other cultures has helped many tourists dispel long-held stereotypes about other nations. — STEREOTYPES (n) = định kiến, khuôn mẫu rập khuôn; collocation "dispel/reinforce stereotypes"; tính từ là "stereotypical", không phải "stereotypic".

9. A society genuinely committed to cultural pluralism must actively support the languages of its smaller communities. — PLURALISM (n) = sự đa nguyên văn hoá; collocation "cultural/religious pluralism", "promote pluralism"; tính từ "pluralistic".

10. Rapid urban development has, in many cases, marginalised indigenous communities, silencing voices that were already faint. — MARGINALISE (v) = gạt ra bên lề; dùng chính tả Anh "marginalise", không phải "marginalize" kiểu Mỹ; collocation "marginalised communities".

11. Countries that embrace multiculturalism, allowing each group to keep its own identity, are often more socially resilient. — MULTICULTURALISM (n) = chủ nghĩa đa văn hoá; đối lập với "assimilation"; collocation "promote multiculturalism", "a multicultural society".

12. Diasporic communities often preserve old customs even more carefully than their counterparts back home. — DIASPORIC (adj) = thuộc về cộng đồng kiều bào/di dân; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ ba "-SPOR-"; danh từ gốc là "diaspora".

passages.text: When the United Nations declared 2022 to 2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages, the announcement was met with the kind of polite consensus that conceals more disagreement than it resolves. Linguists estimate that of the roughly 7,100 languages currently spoken, between forty and fifty per cent are unlikely to outlast the present century in any form that supports daily communication. The policy response, however, is far less settled than the rhetoric of preservation might imply. Whether state programmes can meaningfully arrest language loss has become an instructive controversy in contemporary sociolinguistics, an example of how findings about people and the self travel beyond what the evidence can comfortably bear.

The conventional case for heritage language preservation rests on three interlocking claims. The first, articulated influentially by Professor Suzanne Romaine at the University of Oxford, holds that each language encodes a distinctive ecological and historical knowledge — taxonomies of plants, classifications of weather, navigational vocabularies — that cannot be straightforwardly transposed into a dominant language. The second claim, advanced by sociolinguists working with indigenous communities in the Andes and northern Australia, is that language loss is accompanied by measurable declines in collective wellbeing, particularly among adolescents who report a weakened sense of cultural anchoring. The third, more pragmatic claim, is that public investment in language revitalisation produces measurable returns in school attendance and adult literacy, provided the curriculum is properly integrated.

The Welsh experience is frequently cited as the most successful instance. Statutory protection introduced in 1993, combined with bilingual education and a dedicated television channel, lifted the proportion of children educated through the medium of Welsh from roughly thirteen per cent in 1990 to nearly thirty per cent by 2021. New Zealand's Māori language revitalisation, supported by the kohanga reo or "language nests", and Ireland's far less successful Irish-medium provision, are often discussed alongside Welsh as natural comparisons. Yet the comparison cuts both ways. Dr Caoimhe Ní Bhaoill, a sociolinguist at University College Cork, has argued that the Welsh model rests on conditions — geographical concentration, a literate middle class committed to the language, sustained political will — that are absent in many of the contexts to which it is now exported.

The first sustained challenge to the preservation consensus appeared in the mid-2010s. A research team led by Professor Salikoko Mufwene at the University of Chicago argued that policy debates had focused too narrowly on language as a discrete entity, neglecting the broader sociolinguistic ecologies in which languages live and die. Mufwene contends that, where speakers themselves are systematically deciding not to transmit a language to their children, external preservation programmes risk preserving a museum-piece detached from the communicative life that gives a language its meaning. The argument is not that preservation is wrong, but that the framing in which a language is treated as an object to be saved misconstrues the agency of the speakers. A 2019 meta-review by Hornberger and her colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania, drawing on programmes across thirty-eight countries, found that initiatives imposed without sustained community ownership rarely produced durable gains.

Romaine and her supporters have, in turn, accepted some of these criticisms while resisting others. They concede that paternalistic programmes — those designed by ministries without meaningful consultation — typically founder, and that bare speaker counts are a poor measure of vitality. They argue, however, that the binary between "spontaneous" community decisions and "imposed" state intervention is sometimes overdrawn, because community decisions themselves take place within historical conditions of marginalisation, discrimination and economic pressure that make any choice less than fully free. The distinction matters, in their view, because Mufwene's framing risks normalising as choice what is in fact the residue of prior coercion. Critics have replied that this clarification leaves the precise threshold for legitimate intervention unhelpfully vague.

A separate and arguably more revealing strand of research has shifted the question from preservation to identity. Researchers in cultural psychology, including Professor Hyun-Jin Park of Seoul National University, have argued that the more reliable effect of heritage language exposure lies not in the language as such but in the construction of a coherent sense of self across generations. Long-term interview studies with second-generation Korean Australians and Vietnamese Americans suggest that adolescents who maintain even limited active use of a heritage language report stronger intergenerational attachment, higher self-esteem and a more articulated sense of biographical continuity than peers with comparable exposure who have ceased active use. Such effects are difficult to capture in cross-sectional surveys, but appear with reasonable consistency in qualitative work across continents.

The consequences here are far from negligible. Where the principal benefit of heritage-language work is identity and intergenerational connection rather than measurable fluency, the debates that matter most will centre on dignity, recognition and the legitimacy of multilingual public space, rather than narrowly measured fluency outcomes. The argument calls for more sustained examination than scholars have devoted to it, in the writer's view, partly because it is more resistant to monetisation than enrolment statistics.

Where, then, does this leave the case for heritage languages? Studies of neural plasticity at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics have found that early exposure leaves faint but measurable traces in the brain's phonological circuitry, even among speakers whose everyday fluency has long since faded. Such findings neither vindicate nor condemn state preservation schemes. What they suggest, rather, is that a language is never wholly lost so long as a community chooses to reclaim it — and that the value of preservation cannot be read off fluency statistics alone. The argument, in the end, is as much about belonging and dignity as it is about linguistics.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our cross-cultural psychology series — focusing on the empirical literature concerning bilingual identity construction in immigrant adolescents. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Yuen Tagaloa — that's T-A-G-A-L-O-A, no apostrophe, no hyphen. Tagaloa's 2015 monograph reframed bilingual identity from a binary either-or model into what she calls "dynamic repertoire theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal cohort I'll reference today was first surveyed in 1998 — sorry, let me correct that, 1996; the published descriptive statistics in 1998 covered data collected in 1996. So whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 1996. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Tagaloa's theory USED TO be operationalised with self-report instruments only, NOW the field deploys mixed-methods designs incorporating discourse-analytic transcripts, and from 2027 a multi-country consortium WILL be rolling out neuroimaging modules. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, mixed-methods. Moving to terminology. The bilingual community concept Tagaloa foregrounds — a fluid affiliative grouping that does not require formal membership — is termed "imagined affinity". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: ethnic enclave, diaspora cluster, heritage community. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Tagaloa's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is imagined affinity — i-m-a-g-i-n-e-d affinity. So when the older literature uses ethnic enclave or diaspora cluster, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what sociolinguists call the "language attitude continuum". When ethnographers describe how bilingual adolescents evaluate their heritage tongue against the dominant language, they sketch a graded continuum running from prestige asymmetry through diglossic accommodation to active code-mixing. So, you know, you'll see kids who refuse Mandarin in public but switch back at home — that's diglossic accommodation. Or kids who casually weave Tagalog into English banter mid-sentence — that's code-mixing. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the language attitude continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the survey data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the six hundred adolescents we sampled across four cities last summer, MOST said their heritage language was a source of pride — roughly seventy-eight per cent. Only a few — about nine per cent — described it as a social liability, and some — thirteen per cent — reported neutral or context-dependent attitudes. So pride dominates numerically, but the social-liability tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "identity oscillation". This refers to a temporal pattern in which adolescents cycle between high-affiliation and low-affiliation states with the heritage culture — sometimes within a single week. At Riverside Secondary, our ethnographers recorded seventy-three documented oscillation episodes across the cohort during one academic term. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that integration linearly reduces heritage attachment is, frankly, not supported. Most of the adolescents in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic decline in heritage-language usage as English proficiency increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a U-shaped curve, with a re-engagement spike around ages sixteen to seventeen. So the older "subtractive bilingualism" hypothesis, which predicts linear erosion, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in today's seminar this afternoon. I want you to focus on the transcript-coding protocols specifically, not the neuroimaging futures or the legacy self-report instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: bilingual identity is a dynamic repertoire, not a binary; the technical term for fluid affiliative grouping is imagined affinity; pride dominates heritage-language attitudes at roughly seventy-eight per cent; and subtractive bilingualism is not empirically supported in this cohort. Next week we'll examine bilingual cognition itself. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The three pie charts compare how government heritage funding was distributed across five categories in a European country in 1980, 2000 and 2024.

Overall, the most striking feature is the gradual erosion of funding for tangible monuments in favour of intangible practices and digital archives, producing a far more balanced distribution by the end of the period. Whereas physical monuments commanded the lion's share at the start, no single category dominated by the close of the period.

In 1980, tangible monuments accounted for fully half of all funding, with museums absorbing a further quarter. Intangible practices and digital archives each received a mere 5%, a marginal fraction of the total, while performing arts took 15%. By 2000, monument funding had already contracted to 35%, whereas intangible practices had more than doubled to 12% and digital archives had reached 10%.

By contrast, the 2024 distribution is near-equal: tangible monuments retained only 22%, while intangible practices and digital archives each climbed to 20% and museums held 20%. This near-reversal reflects a substantial reallocation away from physical heritage and towards previously marginal categories.

By the final snapshot, however, the hierarchy had all but collapsed. So thorough was this reallocation that the 2024 distribution constitutes a near-reversal of its 1980 counterpart.

blocks.text: The accelerating pace of globalisation has, beyond doubt, made cultures across the world more similar to one another. Whether this homogenisation is a welcome or harmful development continues to divide opinion. This essay will argue that, while there are clear advantages, the negative consequences are on balance more troubling.

On the positive side, the spread of global media and travel has fostered a more cosmopolitan mindset. It is exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs that has helped to dispel many of the stereotypes once held about other nations. Furthermore, minority cultures occasionally benefit from the global stage: Korean pop music and Japanese cuisine, for example, now enjoy a vast international following that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. In this sense, homogenisation is not entirely a one-way process, since it can amplify previously local voices.

Despite these gains, however, the erosion of indigenous culture appears to me a more serious concern. UNESCO reports that one indigenous language dies every two weeks, taking with it irreplaceable folklore and ecological knowledge. Local crafts and dialects also struggle to compete with cheap, mass-produced goods, while overtourism has reduced authentic rituals in places like Bali to commercialised performances. Pervasive as global brands are, they tend to flatten the distinctive textures of local life into a single, standardised template.

In conclusion, although globalisation has certainly broadened horizons and offered some smaller cultures a global voice, the loss of linguistic and cultural diversity is, in my view, the more pressing issue. Governments should therefore invest in preserving intangible heritage rather than allow market forces alone to determine which traditions survive into the next century.

The proposition that globalisation has triggered a sweeping cultural homogenisation is now an anthropological commonplace. Whether this convergence enriches or impoverishes humanity is, however, far less settled. My position, on balance, is that homogenisation poses a net cultural cost, though its benefits — particularly the dismantling of parochial stereotypes — should not be casually dismissed.

There are, admittedly, defensible reasons to celebrate cultural convergence. Cross-border media flows have broadened cosmopolitan sensibilities and softened the ethnocentrism that historically fuelled xenophobia. It is precisely this expanded horizon that has allowed once-peripheral cultures such as Korean pop, Bollywood cinema and Vietnamese cuisine to attain global currency. Were such exchanges absent, soft power would remain the monopoly of a handful of Western capitals. By the same token, shared norms and lingua francas reduce friction in trade and diplomacy, an efficiency gain whose macroeconomic value is hardly trivial.

Notwithstanding these benefits, the corrosive effects on intangible heritage are, in my considered view, more profound. UNESCO estimates that one indigenous language vanishes fortnightly, eroding ecological wisdom, oral literature and worldviews that no museum can adequately archive. Marginalised indigenous communities find their rituals commodified for tourist consumption, a process that hollows out the very practices it purports to celebrate. Underlying these symptoms is what theorists call the hegemony of Anglo-American consumer norms, a soft imperialism more insidious than any colonial decree precisely because it is willingly internalised.

What is needed, accordingly, is neither nostalgic isolationism nor laissez-faire convergence, but a calibrated cultural policy: state-backed preservation of endangered tongues, robust funding for indigenous arts, and curricula that inculcate appreciation for plurality. Globalisation, properly managed, can be an engine of cross-cultural dialogue; left to market logic alone, it risks producing a flatter, less memorable world in which difference is steadily ironed out.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
Language Extinction: Linguists estimate that one indigenous language dies every two weeks, representing a massive loss of intangible cultural heritage.
The "Global Village" Effect: The internet and global brands (like McDonald's, Starbucks) have created a homogenised youth culture worldwide, often at the expense of local traditions.

Overtourism: Massive influxes of international tourists are physically damaging tangible heritage sites (e.g., Venice, Machu Picchu) and turning authentic local rituals into commercialised performances.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Globalisation (Does it destroy or enrich culture?)
Enrichment (Pros): Fosters a cosmopolitan mindset; reduces ethnocentrism and xenophobia; allows minority cultures to share their art and cuisine with a global audience (e.g., K-pop, sushi).
Destruction (Cons): Leads to cultural homogenisation (Westernization); marginalises indigenous languages; traditional crafts disappear as cheap, mass-produced global goods dominate the market.
Topic: Assimilation vs. Multiculturalism (Should immigrants adopt the host culture?)

For Assimilation: Creates a cohesive society with shared social norms and etiquette; prevents the formation of isolated cultural ghettos; a shared lingua franca (common language) is vital for economic efficiency.

For Multiculturalism (Integration): A "melting pot" society benefits from diverse perspectives and innovations; forcing assimilation violates individual identity and human rights; diversity is a strength, not a weakness.
Topic: Funding the Arts & Heritage (Should governments pay for preservation?)

Arguments FOR: Artefacts and folklore are irreplaceable links to our ancestry; they generate significant revenue through cultural tourism; private companies will not fund preservation if it isn't profitable.

Arguments AGAINST: Public funds should be prioritised for pressing issues like healthcare and tertiary education; some traditions naturally evolve or die out, and attempting to artificially preserve them is futile.
(Mệnh đề nhượng bộ nâng cao - Tuyệt chiêu thể hiện "Critical Thinking" (Tư duy phản biện) trong IELTS Writing)

Cue Card

Prep Notes
RITUAL: ancestral altar offering — Đám giỗ (death anniversary)
WHEN/WHERE: lunar anniversary, ancestral home
WHAT: incense, food offering, family gathering, prayer
WHY: kinship, intangible heritage, antidote to modern atomisation
Model Answer (273 words)

The cultural ritual I find most profoundly meaningful is the Vietnamese death anniversary ceremony, locally known as "đám giỗ" — a deeply rooted observance held on the lunar anniversary of an ancestor's passing. (reduced relative)

The ceremony invariably takes place at the ancestral home, where the family altar — laden with incense, fresh fruit, and the deceased's favourite dishes — becomes the spiritual epicentre of the day. It is at dawn, when the household is still hushed, that the eldest male typically lights the first stick of incense, inviting the ancestor's spirit to partake of the meal. (cleft)

What follows is, by any measure, more than a ritual: it's a convocation of kinship. Relatives I haven't seen in years drift in from neighbouring provinces, bringing children, gossip, and freshly prepared offerings. Were this ritual ever to fall into disuse, an entire web of intergenerational ties would, I suspect, quietly unravel. (conditional inversion)

The reason it resonates with me so deeply is essentially threefold. (cleft) First, steeped in Confucian filial piety, it embodies a worldview in which the dead are not gone but merely transposed — a beautifully non-binary conception of mortality. (reduced relative) Second, not only does it transmit intangible heritage — from dialect to recipe to ritual etiquette — but it also functions as an antidote to the atomisation of modern urban life. (negative inversion + nominalisation) Third, it offers a sense of belonging I'd struggle to find elsewhere.
To borrow an idiom, in our hyper-mobile generation it's easy to drift apart, but đám giỗ is the glue that keeps us tight-knit (informal idiom). Frankly, I'd be culturally adrift without it. (hedging)
Examiner Follow-up
"Do you think younger Vietnamese still value this ritual?"

Suggested response (42 words): Honestly, what concerns me is that urban Gen-Z tend to view it as somewhat archaic. Were the elders not to actively transmit the rituals, much of the meaning would, in all likelihood, be lost within two generations — a sobering thought.

blocks.text: Q1. Is cultural homogenisation inevitable?
P: Cultural homogenisation is, to a considerable extent, a structural feature of late-stage globalisation, but the notion of its inevitability is, I'd argue, somewhat overstated.
E: Global capital, media platforms, and the hegemony of English undeniably push convergence, yet local actors continually indigenise imported forms in ways that defy simple convergence narratives.

E: UNESCO's 2022 World Report on Cultural Diversity noted that of the world's roughly 7,000 languages, 40% are endangered, with one disappearing every fortnight — clear evidence of convergence pressure. Yet the same report highlights the K-pop phenomenon: South Korean cultural exports generated $13.4 billion in 2022 (Korean Foundation for International Cultural Exchange), demonstrating that smaller cultures can also project outwards. Glocalisation, theorised by Roland Robertson, captures this two-way dynamic.
L: Therefore, while homogenising pressures are real, cultures are far more adaptive and porous than the inevitability thesis suggests.
Hedging Toolbox: it would be an oversimplification to claim / there is a strong argument that / contrary to popular belief
Lexical Upgrade Box:
the same → homogenised / uniform
culture → cultural distinctiveness / identity formation
unavoidable → inevitable / structurally embedded
Sample Answer (95 words):

Contrary to popular belief, cultural homogenisation isn't entirely inevitable. UNESCO (2022) flagged that 40% of the world's 7,000 languages are endangered, which does suggest convergence pressure. However, what's often overlooked is the counter-flow: K-pop alone generated $13.4 billion in 2022, proving smaller cultures can project globally. Glocalisation — McDonald's selling rice burgers in Asia — illustrates how local actors reshape what they import. Were governments and communities to actively safeguard intangible heritage, the trajectory could meaningfully diverge. So, while homogenising forces are powerful, deterministic inevitability claims overstate the case.
Q2. Should governments protect minority cultures?
P: Governments bear a strong moral and pragmatic obligation to actively protect minority cultures, though the modalities of such protection must be carefully calibrated to avoid paternalism.
E: Minority cultures embody irreplaceable intangible heritage — linguistic, ecological, philosophical — whose loss is irreversible and impoverishes humanity's collective repertoire.

E: UNESCO's Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage (2003, ratified by 180+ states) explicitly recognises this obligation. The Welsh-language revival offers a striking precedent: targeted educational policy and statutory bilingualism have sustained Welsh speakers at roughly 17.8% of Wales' population (538,300 speakers aged 3+, 2021 Census) — a stabilisation many endangered tongues would envy. New Zealand's Māori revitalisation likewise saw fluent speakers stabilise after state-backed kōhanga reo (language nests). Without intervention, the Endangered Languages Project (2023) estimates 3,000+ languages will vanish this century.
L: Consequently, well-designed state intervention isn't cultural meddling — it's a vital corrective to market forces that would otherwise extinguish minority voices.
Hedging Toolbox: there is a robust case for / on the whole / not without caveats
Lexical Upgrade Box:
protect → safeguard / revitalise
small cultures → minority cultures / marginalised communities
help → subsidise / actively support
Sample Answer (96 words):

There is a robust case for state-led cultural protection. UNESCO's 2003 Convention — ratified by 180+ countries — establishes the principle, and the Endangered Languages Project (2023) warns 3,000+ languages may vanish this century. The Welsh revival, with speakers stabilised at around 17.8% of Wales (538,300 speakers, 2021 Census) thanks to statutory bilingualism, and New Zealand's Māori language nests demonstrate what's achievable when policy is well-designed. Not without caveats, of course: top-down interventions can become tokenistic. Were governments to partner directly with affected communities rather than impose blueprints, the outcomes — both linguistic and cultural — would in all likelihood be far more sustainable.
Q3. Are festivals losing their cultural meaning?
P: Many traditional festivals are, regrettably, undergoing a process of commercial dilution, though the underlying cultural meaning is rarely extinguished outright — it's simply being renegotiated.

E: As festivals are repackaged as tourist spectacles or consumer events, their sacred, communal dimensions get eclipsed by economic logic, yet pockets of authentic practice often persist within the same celebration.

E: UN World Tourism Organisation (UNWTO, 2023) data shows global cultural tourism grew 15% year-on-year post-pandemic, with festivals as a key driver. Venice's Carnevale, for instance, now generates roughly €100 million annually but draws criticism for performative authenticity. Conversely, Bhutan's Tshechu festivals, protected by the kingdom's "high-value, low-impact" tourism policy, remain largely insulated from commercialisation. UNESCO's Living Heritage programme documents both trajectories.
L: Hence, festivals aren't losing their meaning per se — they're being stratified into commercial veneers and protected cores, depending on how communities and policymakers respond.
Hedging Toolbox: to varying degrees / it is fair to say that / there are notable exceptions
Lexical Upgrade Box:
become commercial → succumb to commercialisation / be repackaged
meaning → cultural significance / symbolic weight
real → authentic / unadulterated
Sample Answer (94 words):

It is fair to say that, to varying degrees, festivals are succumbing to commercialisation. UNWTO (2023) reports cultural tourism rebounded 15% year-on-year, with festivals heavily commodified — Venice's Carnevale alone earns €100 million annually but is criticised for performative authenticity. However, there are notable exceptions: Bhutan's Tshechu festivals remain largely insulated thanks to deliberate tourism policy. What this reveals is that meaning isn't lost universally — it's stratified. Were communities given more control over how their festivals are marketed, the authentic core could realistically coexist with tourism revenue, rather than being eclipsed by it.
T05 — CULTURE & IDENTITY (Advanced C1, Band 7.5–8.0)
1. Section Type + Lecturer Info
Section: IELTS Listening Section 4 — formal university lecture, single speaker
Lecturer: Dr. Amara Okonkwo, Department of Cultural Studies
Academic field: Anthropology / Heritage Studies
Topic of lecture: "Cultural Homogenisation, Xenophobia and the Defence of Intangible Heritage in the Age of the Diasporic Self"
2. Pre-listening Vocab Brush-up (Band 7+)
homogenisation (n) — process by which cultures become uniform / indistinguishable
xenophobia (n) — fear or hatred of foreigners
intangible heritage (n phrase) — non-physical cultural assets: folklore, dialects, rituals
diasporic (adj) — relating to communities dispersed from their ancestral homeland
erosion (n) — gradual wearing-away of a tradition or identity
3. Predict 3 Ideas (Advanced)
The lecturer will likely argue that globalisation accelerates the homogenisation of cultures and the erosion of local identity.
She may explore how diasporic communities paradoxically preserve customs better than the homeland.
A warning about rising xenophobia as a backlash against multicultural integration is probable.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

Good morning, all. In our previous session we mapped the contours of multiculturalism; today, I'd like to, um, complicate that picture by examining three intertwined phenomena: cultural homogenisation, the rise of xenophobia, and the urgent question of intangible heritage. [pause]

Let me start with a striking statistic. UNESCO estimates that one indigenous language dies roughly every fortnight. Now, that's not merely a linguistic curiosity — it represents the wholesale loss of folk songs, oral histories, medicinal knowledge, in short, the very fabric of intangible heritage. The driver, in most cases, is the steady erosion of local custom under the weight of globalised consumer culture. [pause]

You'll have noticed, perhaps, that whilst global cuisine and brands flourish, what scholars term cultural homogenisation is quietly hollowing out distinctive regional practices. Towns from Hanoi to Reykjavik now share remarkably similar shopping districts. And, importantly, this erosion is not neutral — it disproportionately marginalises smaller communities whose voices were already faint. [pause]

But here's where the story takes an unexpected turn. Diasporic communities — Vietnamese in Sydney, Greeks in Melbourne, West Africans in Paris — frequently preserve customs more rigorously than their counterparts in the country of origin. Why? Well, the diaspora, isolated from the modernising pressures of the homeland, treats tradition as an anchor of identity, an indispensable marker of self. [pause]

Now, the darker counter-current: as societies grow more cosmopolitan, certain segments of the host population react with xenophobia — that is, an irrational fear of the foreign. Sociologists attribute this not to genuine cultural threat but to economic insecurity and political opportunism. [pause]

Now, I promised you the two agendas were inseparable, but before we get to remedies I want to introduce a wrinkle that the standard narrative tends to airbrush out — namely, that heritage preservation is itself, um, far from innocent. Consider UNESCO's own intangible-heritage listings. A study by the anthropologist Valdimar Hafstein found that the very act of inscribing a folk practice onto a register can paradoxically ossify it — freezing a living, mutating tradition into a museum piece, a performance staged chiefly for tourists. The Jemaa el-Fnaa storytellers of Marrakech are the textbook case: once celebrated on a UNESCO list, the square's oral culture drifted toward spectacle rather than genuine transmission. So safeguarding, done clumsily, can hollow out the thing it claims to rescue. [pause]

A further consideration concerns who gets to speak for a culture. When a state nominates a tradition as "national heritage", it implicitly selects an official version — and minority or dissenting variants are quietly written out. In several post-colonial nations, the dominant ethnic group's customs become the nation's heritage, while the very indigenous languages we were lamenting earlier remain unlisted, unfunded, invisible. Preservation, if you like, can be a subtle instrument of internal homogenisation rather than a cure for it. [pause]

And here's the sharpest irony of all. That same globalised digital infrastructure we blamed for cultural erosion is now, simultaneously, its lifeline. Maori activists have used streaming apps to teach te reo to tens of thousands; Sámi musicians reach global audiences from the Arctic; diasporic Vietnamese maintain ritual calendars through social media. So the homogenising tide and the revival current, frankly, flow through the very same channel. [pause]

Which means the binary I sketched at the outset — globalisation versus tradition — is far too tidy. The real question is one of governance and intent. And that, of course, is precisely where the state cannot stay neutral — let me flag the key policy implication…
In closing, then, governments must invest in safeguarding intangible heritage whilst simultaneously combating xenophobic rhetoric. The two agendas, frankly, are inseparable.

blocks.text: 8. Listening Skills Box

Signposting recognition: "Let me start with…", "But here's where the story takes an unexpected turn", "In closing, then" — these are gold-standard Section 4 anchors. Each typically frames one question.
Lexical reformulation: "indispensable marker / anchor" (Q3) and "inseparable" (Q5) — both are reformulations of "essential / linked". Train your ear for adjective-of-strength substitutions.
Negation contrast cue: Q4 relies on the "not … but …" pattern — almost always the second element is the answer.

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~180 từ)
The three pie charts compare how government heritage funding was distributed across five categories in a European country in 1980, 2000 and 2024.

Overall, the most striking feature is the gradual erosion of funding for tangible monuments in favour of intangible practices and digital archives, producing a far more balanced distribution by the end of the period. Whereas physical monuments commanded the lion's share at the start, no single category dominated by the close of the period.

In 1980, tangible monuments accounted for fully half of all funding, with museums absorbing a further quarter. Intangible practices and digital archives each received a mere 5%, a marginal fraction of the total, while performing arts took 15%. By 2000, monument funding had already contracted to 35%, whereas intangible practices had more than doubled to 12% and digital archives had reached 10%.

By contrast, the 2024 distribution is near-equal: tangible monuments retained only 22%, while intangible practices and digital archives each climbed to 20% and museums held 20%. This near-reversal reflects a substantial reallocation away from physical heritage and towards previously marginal categories.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~180 từ)
The three pie charts illustrate the changing allocation of government heritage funding across five categories in a European country, captured at three points: 1980, 2000 and 2024.

Overall, what stands out is a pronounced redistribution away from tangible monuments and towards previously peripheral categories, such that an initially top-heavy pattern gives way to near-parity. The dominance once enjoyed by physical heritage is steadily dismantled across successive snapshots.

In 1980, it was tangible monuments that commanded the lion's share, absorbing fully half of the budget, with museums constituting a further quarter; intangible practices and digital archives languished at a marginal 5% apiece, and performing arts at 15%. By 2000, monument funding had already retreated to 35%, whereas intangible practices had more than doubled to 12% and digital archives had risen to 10%.

By the final snapshot, however, the hierarchy had all but collapsed. Tangible monuments retained barely 22%, while intangible practices and digital archives had each quadrupled to 20%, matching both museums and performing arts. So thorough was this reallocation that the 2024 distribution constitutes a near-reversal of its 1980 counterpart.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  Mở bài B8 paraphrase mạnh hơn ('captured at three points') và overview dùng nominalisation 'redistribution' thay vì liệt kê đơn giản như B7.
•  B8 chèn cleft ('it was tangible monuments that commanded...') và đảo ngữ kết quả ('So thorough was this reallocation that...'), trong khi B7 chủ yếu dựa vào 'whereas' / 'by contrast'.
•  B8 dùng bội số chính xác ('had each quadrupled') và động từ học thuật ('languished', 'dismantled', 'retreated'), nâng LR + GRA rõ rệt so với B7.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Identify the dominant slice in each pie and note whether the leader changes (monuments lead 1980 and 2000; near-parity by 2024).
•  Find the biggest mover up and down (monuments collapse 50% → 22%; intangible practices quadruple 5% → 20%).
•  Cluster categories into physical heritage (monuments + museums) versus non-physical (intangible + digital + performing).
•  Plan four paragraphs: Intro + Overview (key shift = reallocation) + Body 1 (decliners) + Body 2 (risers / new balance).
•  Always compare across snapshots, not within one pie — reference at least two of the three pies in each body paragraph.

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Positive aspects of homogenisation:
•  Cross-cultural exposure fosters a cosmopolitan mindset and dispels stereotypes, reducing ethnocentrism and xenophobia.
•  Minority cultures can project soft power globally — K-pop, sushi and anime now command audiences unthinkable a generation ago.
•  Shared norms and lingua francas (human-rights vocabulary, ISO standards) facilitate trade, science and diplomacy.
Negative aspects of homogenisation:
•  Intangible heritage is eroding — UNESCO records one indigenous language dying every fortnight, taking folklore and knowledge with it.
•  Indigenous customs are marginalised or commodified, as commercialised tribal tourism in Bali and Hawaii illustrates.
•  A hegemonic monoculture skewed toward Anglo-American norms weakens local artistic traditions and culinary diversity.

•  Body 2 — argue the heavier costs: loss of intangible heritage, commodification of indigenous practice, and the spread of a hegemonic monoculture.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~270 words)

The accelerating pace of globalisation has, beyond doubt, made cultures across the world more similar to one another. Whether this homogenisation is a welcome or harmful development continues to divide opinion. This essay will argue that, while there are clear advantages, the negative consequences are on balance more troubling.

On the positive side, the spread of global media and travel has fostered a more cosmopolitan mindset. It is exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs that has helped to dispel many of the stereotypes once held about other nations. Furthermore, minority cultures occasionally benefit from the global stage: Korean pop music and Japanese cuisine, for example, now enjoy a vast international following that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. In this sense, homogenisation is not entirely a one-way process, since it can amplify previously local voices.

Despite these gains, however, the erosion of indigenous culture appears to me a more serious concern. UNESCO reports that one indigenous language dies every two weeks, taking with it irreplaceable folklore and ecological knowledge. Local crafts and dialects also struggle to compete with cheap, mass-produced goods, while overtourism has reduced authentic rituals in places like Bali to commercialised performances. Pervasive as global brands are, they tend to flatten the distinctive textures of local life into a single, standardised template.

In conclusion, although globalisation has certainly broadened horizons and offered some smaller cultures a global voice, the loss of linguistic and cultural diversity is, in my view, the more pressing issue. Governments should therefore invest in preserving intangible heritage rather than allow market forces alone to determine which traditions survive into the next century.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~293 words)

The proposition that globalisation has triggered a sweeping cultural homogenisation is now an anthropological commonplace. Whether this convergence enriches or impoverishes humanity is, however, far less settled. My position, on balance, is that homogenisation poses a net cultural cost, though its benefits — particularly the dismantling of parochial stereotypes — should not be casually dismissed.

There are, admittedly, defensible reasons to celebrate cultural convergence. Cross-border media flows have broadened cosmopolitan sensibilities and softened the ethnocentrism that historically fuelled xenophobia. It is precisely this expanded horizon that has allowed once-peripheral cultures such as Korean pop, Bollywood cinema and Vietnamese cuisine to attain global currency. Were such exchanges absent, soft power would remain the monopoly of a handful of Western capitals. By the same token, shared norms and lingua francas reduce friction in trade and diplomacy, an efficiency gain whose macroeconomic value is hardly trivial.

Notwithstanding these benefits, the corrosive effects on intangible heritage are, in my considered view, more profound. UNESCO estimates that one indigenous language vanishes fortnightly, eroding ecological wisdom, oral literature and worldviews that no museum can adequately archive. Marginalised indigenous communities find their rituals commodified for tourist consumption, a process that hollows out the very practices it purports to celebrate. Underlying these symptoms is what theorists call the hegemony of Anglo-American consumer norms, a soft imperialism more insidious than any colonial decree precisely because it is willingly internalised.

What is needed, accordingly, is neither nostalgic isolationism nor laissez-faire convergence, but a calibrated cultural policy: state-backed preservation of endangered tongues, robust funding for indigenous arts, and curricula that inculcate appreciation for plurality. Globalisation, properly managed, can be an engine of cross-cultural dialogue; left to market logic alone, it risks producing a flatter, less memorable world in which difference is steadily ironed out.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  B8 mở bài bằng register học thuật ('an anthropological commonplace') và lập trường định lượng tinh tế ('a net cultural cost'), thay vì lập trường phẳng của B7.

•  B8 dày đặc cấu trúc cao cấp: cleft, đảo ngữ điều kiện ('Were such exchanges absent'), fronting ('Underlying these symptoms is'), nominalisation ('the dismantling of parochial stereotypes'); B7 chỉ có một cleft.

•  B8 đề xuất giải pháp cụ thể, ba nhánh ('state-backed preservation ... robust funding ... curricula') và đóng bằng tương phản 'properly managed / left to market logic alone', cho thấy TR sâu hơn B7.

Bản địa, bản xứ, có nguồn gốc từ một vùng đất từ thời xa xưa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> UNESCO estimates that one **indigenous** language dies roughly every fortnight, taking with it irreplaceable folklore and knowledge.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
indi- gợi liên tưởng "in địa" (trong lòng đất/vùng đất đó) → sinh ra và thuộc về nơi đó → bản địa.
vocabulary.common_error: Trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai '-DIG-', chữ 'g' phát âm mềm /dʒ/ chứ không phải /g/ cứng.
vocabulary.definition_en: belonging to or originating from a particular place from earliest known times; native
vocabulary.definition_vi: bản địa, bản xứ
vocabulary.example: UNESCO estimates that one indigenous language dies roughly every fortnight, taking with it irreplaceable folklore and knowledge.
vocabulary.memory_hook: indi- gợi liên tưởng "in địa" (trong lòng đất/vùng đất đó) → sinh ra và thuộc về nơi đó → bản địa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự đồng hoá văn hoá, quá trình một nhóm thiểu số dần tiếp nhận phong tục của nền văn hoá chủ đạo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> New immigrants often experience a process of cultural **assimilation** when adapting to a host country.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
assimilate gần giống "similar" (giống nhau) → trở nên giống với văn hoá chủ đạo → đồng hoá.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'assimilation' (từ bỏ dần bản sắc gốc để hoà vào văn hoá chủ đạo) với 'integration' (hoà nhập nhưng vẫn giữ được bản sắc riêng).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process by which a minority group gradually adopts the customs and attitudes of the dominant culture
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự đồng hoá (văn hoá)
vocabulary.example: New immigrants often experience a process of cultural assimilation when adapting to a host country.
vocabulary.memory_hook: assimilate gần giống 'similar' (giống nhau) → trở nên giống với văn hoá chủ đạo → đồng hoá.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự mai một, xói mòn dần các giá trị hoặc truyền thống văn hoá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The driver of language loss, in most cases, is the steady **erosion** of local custom under the weight of globalised consumer culture.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng đến "erosion" trong địa chất (xói mòn đất đá) → áp dụng cho văn hoá: bị bào mòn dần theo thời gian.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi nói nghĩa bóng, dùng *the erosion of culture/trust/rights*; không dùng động từ *erosion*—động từ là *erode*.
vocabulary.definition_en: the gradual destruction or wearing away of cultural traditions or values
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự mai một, xói mòn (giá trị/truyền thống văn hoá)
vocabulary.example: The driver of language loss, in most cases, is the steady erosion of local custom under the weight of globalised consumer culture.
vocabulary.memory_hook: liên tưởng đến 'erosion' trong địa chất (xói mòn đất đá) → áp dụng cho văn hoá: bị bào mòn dần theo thời gian.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Di sản văn hoá phi vật thể: ca dao, ngôn ngữ, lễ hội, tri thức truyền miệng không có hình thái vật chất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Governments must invest heavily in preserving not only physical artefacts but also **intangible heritage** like folklore and dialects.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
in- (không) + tangible (sờ được) → "không sờ được" → di sản phi vật thể như ca dao, lễ hội, ngôn ngữ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Intangible heritage' (phi vật thể: ca dao, lễ hội, ngôn ngữ) đối lập với 'tangible heritage' (vật thể: di tích, công trình kiến trúc) — cần phân biệt rõ khi viết Writing Task 2.
vocabulary.definition_en: cultural practices, expressions, knowledge and skills passed down through generations but lacking physical form, such as folklore, dialects and rituals
vocabulary.definition_vi: di sản văn hoá phi vật thể
vocabulary.example: Governments must invest heavily in preserving not only physical artefacts but also intangible cultural heritage like folklore and dialects.
vocabulary.memory_hook: in- (không) + tangible (sờ được) → "không sờ được" → di sản phi vật thể như ca dao, lễ hội, ngôn ngữ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Định kiến, khuôn mẫu rập khuôn, những niềm tin đơn giản hoá quá mức về một nhóm người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs has helped to dispel many of the **stereotypes** once held about other nations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
stereo- (cứng, rắn, in khuôn) + type (loại) → "đóng khuôn cứng nhắc" cho một nhóm người → định kiến.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Stereotype' vừa là danh từ vừa là động từ; dạng tính từ là 'stereotypical', không phải 'stereotypic' (ít dùng).
vocabulary.definition_en: oversimplified, widely held beliefs or images about a particular type of person or thing
vocabulary.definition_vi: định kiến, khuôn mẫu rập khuôn
vocabulary.example: Exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs has helped to dispel many of the stereotypes once held about other nations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: stereo- (cứng, rắn, in khuôn) + type (loại) → "đóng khuôn cứng nhắc" cho một nhóm người → định kiến.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vị chủng, có xu hướng đánh giá các nền văn hoá khác dựa trên chuẩn mực của văn hoá mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Cross-border media flows have broadened cosmopolitan sensibilities and softened the **ethnocentrism** that historically fuelled xenophobia.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
ethno- (dân tộc) + centric (lấy làm trung tâm) → coi dân tộc/văn hoá mình là trung tâm, chuẩn mực → vị chủng.
vocabulary.common_error: *Ethnocentric* mô tả quan điểm lấy văn hóa mình làm chuẩn; không dùng như từ thay thế chung cho *patriotic* hay *nationalistic*.
vocabulary.definition_en: evaluating other cultures according to preconceptions originating in the standards and customs of one's own culture, typically with an implicit belief in its superiority
vocabulary.definition_vi: vị chủng, mang tư tưởng lấy văn hoá của mình làm chuẩn mực
vocabulary.example: Cross-border media flows have broadened cosmopolitan sensibilities and softened the ethnocentrism that historically fuelled xenophobia.
vocabulary.memory_hook: ethno- (dân tộc) + centric (lấy làm trung tâm) → coi dân tộc/văn hoá mình là trung tâm, chuẩn mực → vị chủng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự đa nguyên văn hoá, trạng thái nhiều nhóm văn hoá/sắc tộc khác nhau cùng tồn tại trong một xã hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A multicultural society genuinely committed to cultural **pluralism** must actively protect the languages and customs of its smaller communities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
plural (số nhiều, nhiều loại) + -ism → trạng thái nhiều nền văn hoá cùng tồn tại → đa nguyên.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm *pluralism* (sự cùng tồn tại của nhiều nhóm/quan điểm) với *plurality* (số nhiều hoặc số phiếu cao nhất).
vocabulary.definition_en: a condition or system in which multiple distinct cultural, ethnic, or religious groups coexist within one society
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự đa nguyên, đa dạng (văn hoá) cùng tồn tại trong một xã hội
vocabulary.example: A multicultural society genuinely committed to cultural pluralism must actively protect the languages and customs of its smaller communities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: plural (số nhiều, nhiều loại) + -ism → trạng thái nhiều nền văn hoá cùng tồn tại → đa nguyên.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Gạt ra bên lề xã hội, coi nhẹ tiếng nói hoặc vai trò của một nhóm người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This erosion is not neutral — it disproportionately **marginalises** smaller communities whose voices were already faint.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
margin (lề trang giấy) → đẩy ai đó ra "lề" của xã hội → bị gạt ra ngoài, coi nhẹ.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng chính tả Anh 'marginalise' (không phải 'marginalize' kiểu Mỹ) trong bài viết IELTS theo chuẩn British English.
vocabulary.definition_en: to treat a person or group as insignificant or peripheral, pushing them to the edges of society
vocabulary.definition_vi: gạt ra bên lề, coi nhẹ (một nhóm người/nền văn hoá)
vocabulary.example: This erosion is not neutral — it disproportionately marginalises smaller communities whose voices were already faint.
vocabulary.memory_hook: margin (lề trang giấy) → đẩy ai đó ra 'lề' của xã hội → bị gạt ra ngoài, coi nhẹ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chủ nghĩa đa văn hoá, sự cùng tồn tại của nhiều nhóm văn hoá khác nhau trong một xã hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Multiculturalism** allows people from different backgrounds to live together peacefully while maintaining their own distinct identities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
multi- (nhiều) + cultural (văn hoá) + -ism → nhiều nền văn hoá cùng tồn tại → chủ nghĩa đa văn hoá.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'multiculturalism' (nhiều văn hoá cùng tồn tại, giữ bản sắc riêng) với 'assimilation' (một nhóm từ bỏ bản sắc để hoà vào văn hoá chủ đạo) — hai khái niệm thường được đối lập trong đề thi Writing.
vocabulary.definition_en: the presence of, or support for the presence of, several distinct cultural groups within a society, each maintaining its own identity
vocabulary.definition_vi: chủ nghĩa đa văn hoá
vocabulary.example: Multiculturalism allows people from different backgrounds to live together peacefully while maintaining their own distinct identities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: multi- (nhiều) + cultural (văn hoá) + -ism → nhiều nền văn hoá cùng tồn tại → chủ nghĩa đa văn hoá.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Xua tan, xoá bỏ một niềm tin, định kiến hoặc nỗi lo sợ bằng cách chứng minh nó sai.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs that has helped to **dispel** many of the stereotypes once held about other nations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
dis- (làm mất đi) + liên tưởng "spell" (bùa chú) → phá bỏ "bùa" định kiến trong đầu → xua tan.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *dispel a myth/fear/doubt*; không dùng *dispel people* và không thêm *away* vì *dispel* đã mang nghĩa xua tan.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a feeling, belief, or idea disappear, especially by proving it is false or unjustified
vocabulary.definition_vi: xua tan, xoá bỏ (định kiến, nỗi sợ hãi)
vocabulary.example: It is exposure to foreign cuisine, films and customs that has helped to dispel many of the stereotypes once held about other nations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: dis- (làm mất đi) + liên tưởng 'spell' (bùa chú) → phá bỏ 'bùa' định kiến trong đầu → xua tan.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phép tắc xã giao, những quy tắc ứng xử lịch sự được xã hội hoặc cộng đồng quy định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is customary to remove your shoes before entering someone's home in Japan, a small but important point of **etiquette**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Pháp "étiquette" (nhãn dán, quy tắc ghi trên nhãn) → những quy tắc ứng xử được "dán nhãn" quy định sẵn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Etiquette' là danh từ không đếm được, không có số nhiều 'etiquettes'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the customary code of polite behaviour expected within a society or group
vocabulary.definition_vi: phép tắc xã giao, quy tắc ứng xử lịch sự
vocabulary.example: It is customary to remove your shoes before entering someone's home in Japan, a small but important point of etiquette.
vocabulary.memory_hook: gốc Pháp 'étiquette' (nhãn dán, quy tắc ghi trên nhãn) → những quy tắc ứng xử được 'dán nhãn' quy định sẵn.
word_family: etiquette (n, uncountable — no verb/adjective form in common use)

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc về cộng đồng kiều bào, những người sống rải rác bên ngoài quê hương gốc của họ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Diasporic** communities, isolated from the modernising pressures of the homeland, frequently preserve traditions more rigorously than their counterparts back home.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
diaspora (cộng đồng ly tán, gốc Hy Lạp "gieo rắc, phân tán") + -ic → thuộc về những người sống rải rác xa quê hương.
vocabulary.common_error: Trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ ba '-SPOR-'; tránh phát âm sai thành 'die-ASS-porik'.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to communities of people who have been dispersed from their ancestral homeland and now live scattered across other countries
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về cộng đồng kiều bào/di dân sống rải rác xa quê hương
vocabulary.example: Diasporic communities, isolated from the modernising pressures of the homeland, frequently preserve traditions more rigorously than their counterparts back home.
vocabulary.memory_hook: diaspora (cộng đồng ly tán, gốc Hy Lạp 'gieo rắc, phân tán') + -ic → thuộc về những người sống rải rác xa quê hương.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự bá quyền, thế thống trị áp đảo của một nền văn hoá hoặc quốc gia đối với các nền văn hoá khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some theorists call it the **hegemony** of Anglo-American consumer norms, a soft imperialism more insidious than any colonial decree because it is willingly internalised.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng "hedge" (rào chắn) + "money" (tiền) → thế lực áp đảo dùng tiền và rào chắn để thống trị → bá quyền.
vocabulary.common_error: Có hai cách phát âm được chấp nhận trong tiếng Anh Anh: /hɪˈɡem.ə.ni/ hoặc /ˈheɡ.ə.məʊ.ni/, cả hai đều nhấn âm tiết thứ hai.
vocabulary.definition_en: dominance or leadership of one group, culture, or nation over others, especially in a way that shapes norms and values
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự bá quyền, sự thống trị áp đảo (về văn hoá, chính trị)
vocabulary.example: Some theorists call it the hegemony of Anglo-American consumer norms, a soft imperialism more insidious than any colonial decree because it is willingly internalised.
vocabulary.memory_hook: liên tưởng 'hedge' (rào chắn) + 'money' (tiền) → thế lực áp đảo dùng tiền và rào chắn để thống trị → bá quyền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cú sốc văn hoá, cảm giác bối rối, mất phương hướng khi tiếp xúc với một nền văn hoá xa lạ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> When I moved to a foreign country, I experienced severe **culture shock** for the first few months.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
culture (văn hoá) + shock (cú sốc) → cú sốc khi tiếp xúc với văn hoá lạ.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong văn phong học thuật Band 8, có thể nâng cấp thành 'adjustment disequilibrium upon cross-cultural relocation' thay vì lặp lại cụm cơ bản 'culture shock' quá nhiều lần.
vocabulary.definition_en: a feeling of disorientation or confusion experienced when suddenly encountering an unfamiliar culture or way of life
vocabulary.definition_vi: cú sốc văn hoá
vocabulary.example: When I moved to a foreign country, I experienced severe culture shock for the first few months.
vocabulary.memory_hook: culture (văn hoá) + shock (cú sốc) → cú sốc khi tiếp xúc với văn hoá lạ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ chỉ cảm giác lạc lõng, không hợp với hoàn cảnh, giống như cá bị mắc cạn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I didn't know anyone and didn't speak the language; I felt like a **fish out of water**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh con cá bị đưa ra khỏi nước → không thể sống bình thường → cảm giác lạc lõng, không hợp môi trường.
collocations: feel like a fish out of water
like a fish out of water
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là thành ngữ (idiom), không nên dùng trong Writing Task 2 học thuật; phù hợp hơn cho Speaking Part 2/3 để tạo giọng văn tự nhiên.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who feels awkward or out of place in an unfamiliar situation or environment
vocabulary.definition_vi: như cá mắc cạn, lạc lõng, không hợp với hoàn cảnh
vocabulary.example: I didn't know anyone and didn't speak the language; I felt like a fish out of water.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hình ảnh con cá bị đưa ra khỏi nước → không thể sống bình thường → cảm giác lạc lõng, không hợp môi trường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ mang nghĩa "nhập gia tuỳ tục" — khi ở đâu thì nên theo phong tục ở đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I don't usually eat such spicy food, but **when in Rome**, do as the Romans do.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Khi ở Rome, hãy làm như người La Mã → sang xứ nào theo phong tục xứ đó → nhập gia tuỳ tục.
collocations: when in Rome, do as the Romans do
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ này luôn đi kèm vế sau 'do as the Romans do'; không nên cắt ngắn khi trích dẫn trong bài viết trang trọng.
vocabulary.definition_en: a saying meaning one should adopt the customs and behaviour of the place or group one is visiting or living in
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhập gia tuỳ tục
vocabulary.example: I don't usually eat such spicy food, but when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
vocabulary.memory_hook: khi ở Rome, hãy làm như người La Mã → sang xứ nào theo phong tục xứ đó → nhập gia tuỳ tục.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phá vỡ truyền thống, chủ động không làm theo phong tục hay thông lệ đã được thiết lập từ trước.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The young couple decided to **break with tradition** and host their wedding on a beach.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
break (phá vỡ) + tradition (truyền thống) → cắt đứt, không theo lối cũ nữa.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *break with tradition* khi từ bỏ thông lệ; *break a tradition* thường gợi việc vi phạm một truyền thống cụ thể và sắc thái khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: to deliberately stop following an established custom or traditional way of doing something
vocabulary.definition_vi: phá vỡ truyền thống, làm khác đi so với thông lệ cũ
vocabulary.example: The young couple decided to break with tradition and host their wedding on a beach.
vocabulary.memory_hook: break (phá vỡ) + tradition (truyền thống) → cắt đứt, không theo lối cũ nữa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thấm đẫm, đậm đà một đặc tính nào đó, đặc biệt là lịch sử hoặc truyền thống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The ancient temples of Kyoto are deeply **steeped in** history and legend.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nghĩa gốc "steep" là ngâm trà trong nước nóng lâu → thấm đẫm hương vị → nghĩa bóng: thấm đẫm lịch sử/văn hoá.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Steeped in' luôn đi với giới từ 'in', không dùng 'steeped with' hay 'steeped by'.
vocabulary.definition_en: deeply infused or imbued with a particular quality, especially history, tradition or culture
vocabulary.definition_vi: đậm đà, thấm đẫm (lịch sử, truyền thống)
vocabulary.example: The ancient temples of Kyoto are deeply steeped in history and legend.
vocabulary.memory_hook: nghĩa gốc 'steep' là ngâm trà trong nước nóng lâu → thấm đẫm hương vị → nghĩa bóng: thấm đẫm lịch sử/văn hoá.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nồi lẩu văn hoá — nơi nhiều nền văn hoá, sắc tộc khác nhau hoà trộn vào nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> New York is often described as a cultural **melting pot**, bringing together people from all over the globe.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
melting (tan chảy) + pot (nồi) → nhiều nguyên liệu/văn hoá khác nhau tan chảy hoà quyện vào nhau trong một "nồi".
vocabulary.common_error: Trong văn phong học thuật Band 8, nên nâng cấp thành 'a polycentric cultural matrix' hoặc 'a layered cosmopolitan tapestry' để tránh lặp lại thành ngữ quá phổ biến này.
vocabulary.definition_en: a place, typically a country or city, where a wide variety of cultures, ethnicities, or ideas are mixed together
vocabulary.definition_vi: nồi lẩu văn hoá, nơi hội tụ nhiều nền văn hoá khác nhau
vocabulary.example: New York is often described as a cultural melting pot, bringing together people from all over the globe.
vocabulary.memory_hook: melting (tan chảy) + pot (nồi) → nhiều nguyên liệu/văn hoá khác nhau tan chảy hoà quyện vào nhau trong một 'nồi'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự phân mảnh, cô lập hoá — quá trình xã hội tan rã thành các cá nhân rời rạc, mất đi sự gắn kết chung.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The death anniversary ceremony functions as an antidote to the **atomisation** of modern urban life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
atom (nguyên tử, đơn vị nhỏ nhất) + -isation → xã hội bị chia nhỏ thành từng cá nhân rời rạc như những nguyên tử tách biệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong xã hội học, *atomisation* là sự phân rã thành cá nhân cô lập; không dùng thay cho *automation* hoặc nghĩa vật lý nếu không có ngữ cảnh.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process by which a society or community breaks down into isolated individuals, losing collective bonds and shared identity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phân mảnh, cô lập hoá (xã hội hiện đại thành các cá nhân rời rạc)
vocabulary.example: The death anniversary ceremony functions as an antidote to the atomisation of modern urban life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: atom (nguyên tử, đơn vị nhỏ nhất) + -isation → xã hội bị chia nhỏ thành từng cá nhân rời rạc như những nguyên tử tách biệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự địa phương hoá toàn cầu — khi sản phẩm/ý tưởng toàn cầu được điều chỉnh cho phù hợp với văn hoá địa phương.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Glocalisation** — McDonald's selling rice burgers in Asia — illustrates how local actors reshape what they import.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
global (toàn cầu) + local (địa phương) ghép lại → toàn cầu hoá nhưng vẫn điều chỉnh theo bản sắc địa phương.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Glocalisation' là từ ghép (global + local), khác với 'globalisation' — cần phân biệt rõ hai khái niệm khi lập luận trong Speaking Part 3.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process by which globally distributed products, ideas, or brands are adapted to fit local cultures and tastes
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự địa phương hoá toàn cầu (kết hợp giữa toàn cầu hoá và bản địa hoá)
vocabulary.example: Glocalisation — McDonald's selling rice burgers in Asia — illustrates how local actors reshape what they import.
vocabulary.memory_hook: global (toàn cầu) + local (địa phương) ghép lại → toàn cầu hoá nhưng vẫn điều chỉnh theo bản sắc địa phương.
